claims.text: Native PGM nanocatalysts have naturally formed surface oxide layers under the relevant initial conditions.
The electronic and adsorption properties of PGM catalyst surfaces govern activity during ethanol oxidation.
The electronic and adsorption properties of PGM catalyst surfaces govern selectivity during ethanol oxidation.
The electronic and adsorption properties of PGM catalyst surfaces govern durability during ethanol oxidation.
A tailored coating can alter the catalyst's native passivation layer.
The engineered coating alters the local electronic environment at catalytically active sites.
The engineered coating modifies adsorbate interactions at the catalyst surface.
The coating reduces formation of over-oxidized catalyst states that would otherwise deactivate the catalyst.
The coating changes the adsorption-desorption kinetics of ethanol and its reaction intermediates.
Changes in adsorbate kinetics caused by the coating favor selected reactive intermediates in the complete ethanol-oxidation pathway.
Coated catalysts will exhibit higher current densities than uncoated catalysts under identical ethanol-oxidation conditions.
Coated catalysts will show greater selectivity toward complete ethanol oxidation than uncoated catalysts.
Coated catalysts will undergo less surface degradation over time than uncoated catalysts.
The proposed coating effect should apply at typical operando potentials for ethanol oxidation.
At extreme potentials, coating degradation or alternative reaction pathways may diminish or eliminate the coating's performance effect.
The magnitude of performance improvement depends on coating thickness, composition, application method, and operational stability.
